title: Modern C#
summary: By the end, your developers write C# that's shorter, clearer and safer by using the language's recent improvements. More readability, fewer bugs.
audience: .NET developers who already write C# and want to master the language's recent improvements to write shorter, safer code.
objectives: Use records, primary constructors and collection expressions to cut down on repetitive code
Simplify properties and extensions with the field keyword and extension members (C# 14)
Write exhaustive pattern matching with advanced switch expressions
Model a result or an error without exceptions using unions and closed types (C# 15, .NET 11)
Decide between a source generator and hand-written code, and adapt asynchronous code with ValueTask and runtime async

modules.title: Records, primary constructors and collection expressions
points: Records and immutable types: value equality, with-expressions, positional records
Primary constructors on classes and structs to cut down wiring code
Collection expressions ([...]) and their implicit conversion to arrays, lists and custom types
modules.workshop: Refactor an existing DTO class into a record with a primary constructor and collection expressions, then verify value equality in tests.

modules.title: Extension members, field and advanced pattern matching
points: Extension members to extend an existing type with properties, not just methods
The field keyword (C# 14) to simplify properties that carry validation logic
Advanced pattern matching: list patterns, relational patterns, combinations with and/or/not
Exhaustive switch expressions checked by the compiler
modules.workshop: Rewrite a chain of validation if/else statements as a switch expression with combined pattern matching, and add a computed property using field.

modules.title: Unions, closed types and source generators
points: Unions and closed hierarchies (C# 15, .NET 11) to represent a result or an error without exceptions
Exhaustiveness of handling checked by the compiler on closed types
What a source generator does: what it automates, and where it avoids reflection-based code
modules.workshop: Replace a hand-rolled result hierarchy with a C# 15 union and verify exhaustive handling at compile time.

modules.title: Modern async: ValueTask and runtime async
points: When to prefer ValueTask over Task to reduce allocations
What runtime async changes: state machines moved into the runtime
Common async pitfalls: ConfigureAwait, async void, deadlocks
modules.workshop: Convert a frequently called async method to ValueTask and measure the drop in allocations on a real scenario.

prerequisites: Basic C#, ability to read object-oriented code.
evaluation: A short quiz at the end of every module, and a wrap-up exercise at the end of the course: refactor a representative code sample using the language's recent improvements.

faq.question: Do we need to already know C# 12 or 13 to take this course?
faq.answer: No. The prerequisites are a working knowledge of basic C# and the ability to read object-oriented code; recent features are introduced one at a time, with their context.

faq.question: Does the course cover .NET 11 as well as C# 15?
faq.answer: The module on unions and closed types relies on C# 15 and .NET 11, but most of the content applies from .NET 10 onwards.

faq.question: Can we work on our own code?
faq.answer: In-house, yes: the exercises can use an excerpt from your codebase. In an inter-company session we start from representative examples.

title: ASP.NET Core 10, fundamentals
summary: By the end, your team can design, configure and run a production-ready web application with ASP.NET Core 10.
audience: .NET developers comfortable with modern C# who are new to ASP.NET Core and need to build a web application end to end.
objectives: Start an ASP.NET Core 10 application with the generic host and understand its startup lifecycle
Design endpoints with routing and minimal APIs
Organise an application's dependencies with dependency injection and the Options pattern
Build a controlled middleware pipeline, in the right order
Connect a database with EF Core 10, and handle configuration, secrets and structured logging

modules.title: Generic host and app startup
points: Role of the generic host (WebApplicationBuilder) and the startup lifecycle of an ASP.NET Core 10 app
Environments (Development, Staging, Production) and how they affect configuration
Organising Program.cs for an application that is going to grow
modules.workshop: Start a minimal ASP.NET Core 10 application and vary its behaviour by execution environment.

modules.title: Routing and minimal APIs
points: Defining endpoints with minimal APIs: verbs, route parameters, binding
Grouping endpoints with MapGroup to share filters and metadata
When to prefer minimal APIs over classic MVC controllers
modules.workshop: Build a small task-management API with grouped endpoints and a shared validation filter.

modules.title: Dependency injection and options
points: Service lifetimes: singleton, scoped, transient, and the traps of mixing them
The Options pattern for strongly typed, validated configuration
Registering and resolving services in the built-in container
modules.workshop: Configure a service with the validated Options pattern and demonstrate the effect of a wrong lifetime choice.

modules.title: Middleware pipeline
points: Role and order of the middleware pipeline, and why that order matters
Writing a custom middleware for a cross-cutting need (logging, header, timing)
Common built-in middleware: exception handling, HTTPS redirection, static files
modules.workshop: Write a middleware that measures each request's processing time and place it correctly in the pipeline.

modules.title: EF Core 10, first contact
points: Configuring a DbContext and registering it in the dependency container
Modelling a first entity and generating its initial migration
Reading and writing data from a minimal API endpoint
modules.workshop: Wire an EF Core 10 DbContext into the task-management API and persist the tasks created.

modules.title: Configuration, secrets and structured logging
points: Configuration sources and their priority order (appsettings, environment, secrets)
User secrets in development, without committing them to the repository
Structured logging with the built-in providers and meaningful log levels
modules.workshop: Add a user secret for an API key and log its use with a structured log entry, without ever writing it in plain text.

prerequisites: Modern C#, HTTP basics.
evaluation: A short quiz at the end of every module, and a walkthrough on the last day: the application built during the course must start, expose its endpoints and persist data.

faq.question: Do we need prior knowledge of ASP.NET Core MVC?
faq.answer: No, the course starts from scratch on ASP.NET Core itself; only a working knowledge of modern C# and HTTP basics are expected.

faq.question: Does the course cover GraphQL APIs or advanced security?
faq.answer: No, those topics are covered in dedicated courses (API design, securing ASP.NET Core and Blazor); here the goal is to master the fundamentals.

faq.question: Is the EF Core module enough for a production project?
faq.answer: It lays the groundwork (DbContext, migration, reading and writing); for advanced modelling and performance, the Entity Framework Core 10 course builds on this module.

audience: .NET developers and tech leads with hands-on ASP.NET Core experience who need to take an application to production with confidence.

Authorise access finely with policies and claims
Make an application observable with OpenTelemetry, correlated logs and metrics
Optimise performance with benchmarks, caching and response compression
Make releases reliable with integration tests and a controlled deployment

JWT tokens: issuing, validation, expiry and renewal
Delegated authentication with OIDC against an identity provider

Custom authorization handlers for specific business rules
Resource-based authorization when a policy alone is not enough

Application metrics that matter in production, beyond system metrics
Correlating logs, traces and metrics to diagnose an incident

modules.title: Performance: benchmarks, caching, compression
points: Measuring before optimising with BenchmarkDotNet
In-memory and distributed caching, and their respective use cases
Response compression and its real effect on load and latency

modules.title: Integration testing with WebApplicationFactory
points: Starting the application in memory with WebApplicationFactory
Replacing external dependencies (database, services) for reproducible tests
Writing integration tests that cover the middleware pipeline and authorization

modules.title: Deployment and controlled hot-reload
points: Deployment strategies (rolling, blue-green) and their effect on availability
Hot-reload in development versus controlled redeployment in production
Feature flags to ship without switching a feature on immediately

evaluation: A short quiz at the end of every module, and a wrap-up scenario on the last day: secure, instrument and deploy a supplied application, with integration tests passing.

faq.question: Do we need to choose between JWT and OIDC before the course?
faq.answer: No, the first module compares the approaches; you leave with criteria suited to your context, not a single imposed answer.

faq.question: Does the course cover Keycloak or Microsoft Entra ID in detail?
faq.answer: It introduces OIDC generically; detailed integration with Keycloak or Microsoft Entra ID is covered in depth in the Securing ASP.NET Core and Blazor course.

faq.question: Do we work on a real application?
faq.answer: In-house, the exercises can use one of your own applications; in an inter-company session we start from a representative sample application.

title: Designing robust web APIs with ASP.NET Core
summary: By the end, your teams ship clear, documented, versioned and secure APIs that your partners and apps consume with no nasty surprises.
audience: .NET developers and tech leads who design APIs consumed by partners or other teams and want to avoid nasty surprises on the consumer side.
objectives: Choose between REST and GraphQL based on context rather than habit
Design validated endpoints with consistent errors in the ProblemDetails format
Document an API with built-in OpenAPI and generate clients from that documentation
Evolve an API without breaking its consumers through versioning
Secure, govern and make a production API reliable: authentication, rate limiting, idempotency and publishing

modules.title: REST or GraphQL: which one, and when

Coexistence of both styles within the same information system
What each style makes easier, and what it makes harder

modules.title: Minimal APIs and controllers, validation and ProblemDetails
points: Minimal APIs versus controllers: decision criteria for an API
Input validation and consistent error responses
The ProblemDetails format to standardise error responses
Grouping several validation errors into a single response
modules.workshop: Add strict validation to an existing endpoint and surface the errors in ProblemDetails format.

modules.title: Built-in OpenAPI, documentation and client generation
points: Native generation of the OpenAPI specification from the code
Enriching documentation with examples and descriptions useful to consumers
Generating a typed client from the OpenAPI specification
modules.workshop: Generate a client from the API's OpenAPI specification and use it to consume an endpoint.

modules.title: Versioning and backward compatibility
points: Versioning strategies: in the URL, the header or the media type
Evolving a contract without breaking existing consumers
Deprecation policy for an API version
modules.workshop: Introduce a new version of an endpoint while keeping the previous version available.

modules.title: Authentication, authorization and rate limiting
points: Authenticating API consumers (API key, token, OIDC)
Authorising based on the consumer's role or subscription plan
Rate limiting to protect the API from abusive usage
modules.workshop: Add a rate-limiting policy to a sensitive endpoint and verify the behaviour once the quota is exceeded.

modules.title: Idempotency, pagination and webhooks
points: Making a creation endpoint idempotent to support retries
Consistent pagination for large collections
Webhooks: delivering an event reliably to the consumer
modules.workshop: Make a creation endpoint idempotent using a client-supplied key, and verify there is no duplicate on a retry.

modules.title: Publishing and governance with Azure API Management
points: Role of an API gateway: publishing, quotas, cross-cutting policies
Publishing an existing API through Azure API Management
Multi-team governance: who exposes what, under which rules
modules.workshop: Publish the API built during the course behind Azure API Management with a quota policy.

prerequisites: ASP.NET Core fundamentals or equivalent experience.
evaluation: A short quiz at the end of every module, and a final review of an API built during the course: versioned contract, consistent errors, documentation and publishing.

faq.question: Do we need an Azure account for the API Management module?
faq.answer: No, the exercise uses a free tier or a shared instance provided during the course; if you already have a subscription, we use that instead.

faq.question: Does the course choose GraphQL or REST for us?
faq.answer: No, the goal is to give you the decision criteria; the hands-on exercises use REST, the style most common in partner contexts.

faq.question: Can we apply these practices to an API already in production?
faq.answer: Yes, and that is the most common in-house setup: the versioning and governance exercises then start from your existing API contract.

title: Securing ASP.NET Core and Blazor
summary: By the end, your teams close the common holes in their ASP.NET Core and Blazor apps, and handle authentication and authorization properly, with Keycloak or Microsoft Entra ID.
audience: .NET developers and tech leads who need to close the common holes in their ASP.NET Core and Blazor applications and put solid authentication and authorization in place.
objectives: Spot and fix the most common OWASP Top 10 flaws in an ASP.NET Core application
Set up OIDC authentication with Keycloak or Microsoft Entra ID
Define fine-grained authorization through policies, resources and multi-tenancy
Know where tokens live depending on the Blazor render mode used (Server, WebAssembly, SSR)
Harden an application with security headers, CSP, CORS, antiforgery, secrets and Data Protection

modules.title: OWASP Top 10 applied to ASP.NET Core
points: Overview of the OWASP Top 10 and its concrete translation in an ASP.NET Core application
Injection, broken access control and security misconfiguration: the most frequent findings in review
Prioritising fixes based on the application's actual exposure
modules.workshop: Audit a supplied application and classify its flaws by OWASP Top 10 category.

modules.title: OIDC authentication with Keycloak or Microsoft Entra ID
points: OIDC flow: authorization code, access and ID tokens, refresh
Configuring Keycloak as an identity provider for an ASP.NET Core application
Configuring Microsoft Entra ID as an alternative, and what changes between the two
Common pitfalls: redirect URI, issuer validation, silent expiry
modules.workshop: Wire an ASP.NET Core application to Keycloak over OIDC and verify the behaviour when the token expires.

modules.title: Fine-grained authorization: policies, resources, multi-tenancy
points: Policies based on claims rather than fixed roles
Resource-based authorization when a policy alone is not enough
Isolating data and rights in a multi-tenant context
modules.workshop: Write a policy that stops a user from one tenant accessing a resource belonging to another tenant.

modules.title: Blazor Server, WebAssembly and SSR: where tokens live
points: Token lifecycle in Blazor Server, server-side only
Token exposure in Blazor WebAssembly, on the client, and its implications
SSR rendering and interactive components: what changes for authentication
modules.workshop: On a given Blazor application, identify where the token is actually stored depending on the render mode used.

modules.title: Security headers, CSP, CORS and antiforgery
points: Essential security headers and what they actually prevent
A Content Security Policy suited to a Blazor application without breaking interactivity
CORS: opening exactly what is needed, no more
Antiforgery protection on forms and state-changing calls
modules.workshop: Set up a restrictive CSP on a Blazor application and fix the violations it reveals.

modules.title: Secrets, Data Protection and encryption
points: Storing secrets outside the code and the repository
The Data Protection API to encrypt sensitive data server-side
Key rotation and its effect on data already encrypted
modules.workshop: Encrypt a piece of sensitive data with Data Protection and verify it still decrypts after a key rotation.

modules.title: Security testing and dependency review
points: Automated tests targeting authentication and authorization
Reviewing dependencies to spot known vulnerabilities
Integrating these checks into a continuous delivery pipeline
modules.workshop: Add a vulnerable-dependency check to a continuous integration pipeline and fix the alert it raises.

prerequisites: ASP.NET Core fundamentals or equivalent experience.
evaluation: A short quiz at the end of every module, and a final audit of a supplied application: OWASP flaws fixed, OIDC authentication working, security headers in place.

faq.question: Does the course guarantee an invulnerable application?
faq.answer: No, no course can guarantee that. The goal is to close the most common flaws and build review habits, not to certify absolute security.

faq.question: Do we need to choose between Keycloak and Microsoft Entra ID before the course?
faq.answer: No, the authentication module covers both; you leave with the criteria to choose based on your context.

faq.question: Does the course cover Blazor Server, WebAssembly and SSR rendering?
faq.answer: Yes, the dedicated module compares the three render modes from the standpoint of token security.

Master a component's lifecycle and rendering to avoid unnecessary re-renders
Share application state with cascading values and scoped services
Choose between Blazor Server and WebAssembly based on the project's constraints
Interoperate with JavaScript and ship an AOT-compiled WebAssembly application within its bundle budget

Event callbacks (EventCallback) between a child and a parent component
Component content (RenderFragment) for generic components

ShouldRender and StateHasChanged to control rendering

Choosing between local state, cascading and a service based on the actual scope needed

Isolating JS interop in a service rather than scattering it across components
Prerendering resources to reduce time to first render

Bundle reduction techniques: trimming, lazy loading of assemblies

faq.question: Does the course cover Blazor Hybrid?
faq.answer: It mentions its existence, but most of the time is spent on Server and WebAssembly, the models most used for web applications.

faq.question: Do you cover token security depending on the render mode?
faq.answer: Briefly across the modules; the topic is covered in depth in the Securing ASP.NET Core and Blazor course.

objectives: Decide where and why to introduce CQRS, without applying it everywhere on principle

modules.title: CQRS: why, when, how

faq.question: Does CQRS force us into two databases?

faq.question: Do we need a message broker already?

faq.question: Do we work on our own code?

objectives: Inventory an Azure DevOps estate and choose between a big-bang cutover and coexistence
Migrate repositories and their history with GitHub Enterprise Importer

Plan and run a cutover without interrupting delivery

faq.question: Can we work on our actual Azure DevOps organisation?
faq.answer: In-house, yes: we start from an export or a copy of your organisation. In an inter-company session we start from a representative sample.

faq.question: Does GitHub Actions Importer convert everything automatically?
faq.answer: No. It converts common tasks and flags what needs manual rework; the course covers both.

faq.question: What happens to our Azure Boards history?
faq.answer: You can keep Azure Boards, integrate it with GitHub, or migrate the backlog to GitHub Projects: the course covers the trade-offs of each option.
